analysis.one_liner: Requires hospitals and clinics to switch to safety needles and needleless systems to protect health workers.
analysis.headline: The bill drew 187 cosponsors from both parties but never received a House vote and died when the 106th Congress ended in January 2001.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have directed OSHA to rewrite its bloodborne pathogens rule to require employers to use needleless systems and needles with built-in safety features instead of ordinary sharps. It would have required front-line health care workers to help choose those devices, forced employers to keep a detailed log of every needlestick, and created a national database and injury-tracking system at NIOSH. It also would have made the rules apply to hospitals exempt from OSHA by tying them to Medicare participation.
analysis.who_benefits: Nurses, phlebotomists, and other direct-care health workers who risk infection with HIV, hepatitis B, and hepatitis C from an accidental needlestick.

how_it_helps.text: Requires employers to use needleless systems and sharps with engineered safety protections instead of ordinary needles, the intervention shown to reduce accidental sticks.
Requires that non-managerial direct-care workers participate in identifying and evaluating the safety devices, so the people actually handling needles have a say in which ones are used.
Requires a separate contaminated-sharps injury log recording when, where, and how each stick happened, giving workers and regulators a record of the hazard.
Directs NIOSH to build a national database of safer devices, evaluation criteria, training materials, and a national system to collect needlestick injury data, with $15 million authorized.
Closes a gap by requiring OSHA-exempt hospitals to comply with the standard as a condition of Medicare participation, so state and religious hospital workers are covered too.

analysis.who_pays: Hospitals, clinics, and other employers with workers exposed to blood, who would bear the cost of buying safer devices, training staff, and maintaining injury logs.

drawbacks.text: Compliance costs: employers would have to purchase needleless systems and safety-engineered devices, which cost more than conventional needles, and retrain staff on each device.
The bill imposes significant recordkeeping: a separate sharps injury log with detailed incident information on top of existing OSHA 200 logging, adding paperwork for employers.

Safety devices are not ideal for every procedure, which the bill acknowledges through an exemption for employers who demonstrate a device does not promote employee or patient safety, interferes with a medical procedure, or is not commercially available — an exemption that required case-by-case judgment.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The protection is real and targeted: a single needlestick can transmit HIV or hepatitis, and safer devices directly prevent those exposures. The costs fall on hospitals and clinics in equipment, training, and paperwork, and the bill's exemption language tries to spare cases where a safety device would compromise care. On balance the benefits to workers' lives and health outweigh the compliance costs, though the paperwork burden is nontrivial for smaller employers.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to three House committees and their subcommittees, never got a floor vote, and died when the 106th Congress ended in January 2001 — though Congress passed a nearly identical Needlestick Safety and Prevention Act that was signed into law in November 2000.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on May 20, 1999, and referred to the Committees on Education and the Workforce, Commerce, and Ways and Means.

By early June 1999 it had been referred to subcommittees — the Subcommittee on Health, the Subcommittee on Workforce Protections, and the Subcommittee on Health and Environment — and no further action was taken.
It accumulated 187 cosponsors, including 34 Republicans and 1 Independent alongside 152 Democrats, but never received a committee markup or floor vote before the Congress ended.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: In the short run, employers avoided the compliance costs of switching to safety devices. Health care workers ultimately came out ahead anyway: Congress passed and the President signed a nearly identical needlestick safety law in November 2000, in the same Congress.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Health care workers, via a successor law

for.name: Rep. Fortney Pete Stark
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on May 20, 1999 and delivered introductory remarks.

for.name: Reps. Marge Roukema, George Miller, and Rob Andrews
for.what_they_did: Joined Stark as original cosponsors at introduction, giving the bill bipartisan sponsorship from the start.

for.name: 187 House members (152 D, 34 R, 1 I)
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, a large bipartisan show of support that never translated into floor action.

against.name: House Education and the Workforce Committee
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to its Health Subcommittee on May 27, 1999 and never scheduled a markup or vote.

against.name: House Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to its Health and Environment Subcommittee on June 15, 1999 and never acted on it.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the referral for provisions within its jurisdiction and took no action on the bill.

sides.party_line_note: Support was bipartisan — 187 cosponsors including 34 Republicans and 1 Independent — and no one voted against it on the record; the bill simply died in committee without a vote, so party lines were never tested.

industries.note: Employers would have had to buy more expensive safety-engineered needles, retrain staff, and keep detailed injury logs. The mandate's cost falls on them, while the protection goes to their employees — which is why the bill's fate mattered to their bottom line. The Medicare condition-of-participation provision (Sec. 5) extended the cost to hospitals otherwise exempt from OSHA.

industries.industry: Medical device makers of safety needles and needleless systems
industries.note: A federal mandate to replace ordinary needles with needleless systems and sharps with engineered protections would have created a large guaranteed market for manufacturers of these devices. In this case, the industry's gain ran alongside worker safety, since the products are the mechanism of protection.
